subtitle: How classic search scores pages by the words they contain, why rare words count for more, how BM25 caps repetition and adjusts for length, and what Google says about keyword stuffing.
outcomes: Explain the move from matching documents to scoring them
Say which terms tf-idf weights most and least
Describe what BM25's k1 and b parameters do
Write without a keyword density target
intro: Before neural ranking, search engines scored pages by the words they shared with the query. Those ideas still run most site search tools, and they explain why repeating a keyword stops helping.

This course uses the textbook Introduction to Information Retrieval, Robertson and Zaragoza's review of BM25, Google's spam policies, and a Search Engine Journal report of comments by Google's John Mueller.
The textbook and review describe methods. None of these sources says what Google or Bing use. Advice beyond the sources' words is labelled practitioner judgement.

lessons.title: From matching to scoring
objectives: Explain why match or no match isn't enough
Describe the bag of words model

beats.caption: In Boolean search, a document either matches or does not match a query.
The number of matching documents can far exceed what a person could sift through.
Bag of words: the order of terms is ignored, but the number of occurrences of each term is material.
The vector space model represents queries as vectors in the same space as the documents.
Similarity can be measured as the cosine of the angle between two vectors.

blocks.text: In a Boolean model, the textbook says, a document either matches or does not match a query. The trouble is that the resulting number of matching documents can far exceed the number a human user could possibly sift through.
So search engines need a score that puts the best matches first.
The bag of words model is the simplest way to score. The exact ordering of the terms in a document is ignored, but the number of occurrences of each term is material.
Hypothetical: 'grey sofa, grey cushions' becomes grey 2, sofa 1, cushions 1. 'Cushions grey, sofa grey' gives the same counts.
The vector space model treats each document as a vector, with one component for each dictionary term, and represents queries as vectors in the same space.

Two documents with very similar content can have a big vector difference just because one is longer. To compensate for document length, the textbook's standard measure is cosine similarity: the cosine of the angle between the two vectors.

blocks.label: Textbook note
blocks.text: The textbook mentions that search engines have offered this as a 'more like this' feature in results lists. That doesn't tell you how any engine ranks today.

takeaways.text: Boolean search only says match or no match.
Too many documents can match to sift through.
Bag of words drops order but keeps counts.
Cosine similarity compares the angle between vectors.

exercise.title: Count your words
steps: Copy the opening paragraph of one of your pages.
List each distinct word with how often it appears.
Shuffle the paragraph's sentences and count again.
Note that the counts are the same, which is all bag of words sees.
exercise.prompt_template: Here is a paragraph from my page: [paragraph]. Using the textbook's bag of words model (order ignored, counts kept), list each term and its count, then tell me which words a query like [query] would share with it. Note this is a teaching model, not how Google ranks.

reflection: Which words on your page would any page on the topic use?
What does word order tell a reader that counts don't?
lessons.whats_next: Next, how tf-idf decides which words carry the most weight.

lessons.title: Tf-idf: weighting terms
objectives: Say which terms tf-idf weights highest
Say which terms it weights lowest

beats.caption: Tf-idf gives a composite weight for each term in each document.
The weight is highest when a term occurs many times within a small number of documents.
It is lower when the term occurs fewer times in a document, or occurs in many documents.
It is lowest when the term occurs in virtually all documents.
That's idf at work: the idf of a rare term is high, and the idf of a frequent term is likely to be low.

blocks.text: Tf-idf combines two counts into a composite weight for each term in each document. Term frequency (tf) is how often the term appears in the document. Inverse document frequency (idf) reflects how many documents in the collection contain it.
The textbook says the idf of a rare term is high, whereas the idf of a frequent term is likely to be low.
The textbook describes three cases.

items.text: The term occurs many times within a small number of documents.
The term occurs fewer times in a document, or occurs in many documents.
The term occurs in virtually all documents.

blocks.text: Hypothetical sofa shop: 'chesterfield' appears often on three pages, so it scores high on those pages. 'the' is on every page, so it scores lowest everywhere.

blocks.label: Practitioner judgement
blocks.text: The distinctive words of your topic are the ones a tf-idf style score rewards. Generic words that every page uses add little. This is an inference from the textbook, not a statement about Google.

takeaways.text: Tf-idf gives each term a weight per document.
Many uses in few documents scores highest.
Terms in almost every document score lowest.
Rare terms have a high idf.

exercise.title: Find your distinctive terms
steps: Pick a topic you cover on several pages.
List words that appear on almost every page of your site.
List words that appear only on the pages about this topic.
Check that the second list shows up in your headings and copy.
exercise.prompt_template: My site has these pages: [titles]. For the topic [topic], suggest which terms would have a high idf on my site (used on few pages) and which would have a low idf (used everywhere), using the textbook's tf-idf idea. Label it as an illustration, not how Google ranks.

reflection: Which words appear on every page of your site?
Which terms only your best page on a topic uses?
lessons.whats_next: Next, BM25: how repetition saturates and length is normalised.

lessons.title: BM25: saturation and length
objectives: Say what k1 and b control

beats.caption: BM25 is the best-known instantiation of a term-weighting and document-scoring function.
Any one term's contribution to the score cannot exceed a saturation point.
k1 calibrates term frequency scaling. A k1 of 0 is a binary model, with no term frequency.
b = 1 fully scales the term weight by document length. b = 0 means no length normalization.
Proximity: the smallest window containing all the query terms. The smaller it is, the better the match.

blocks.text: Robertson and Zaragoza call BM25 the best-known instantiation of their model: a term-weighting and document-scoring function. In it, any one term's contribution to the document score cannot exceed a saturation point.
So the first few uses of a term add the most, and each extra repeat adds less.
The textbook describes two tuning parameters.

items.text: A positive tuning parameter that calibrates document term frequency scaling. A k1 of 0 corresponds to a binary model, with no term frequency.
Controls length. b = 1 fully scales the term weight by document length; b = 0 corresponds to no length normalization.

blocks.text: The review says document-length normalisation is critical to the model.

Scores can also look at proximity. The textbook uses the width of the smallest window in a document that contains all the query terms. Intuitively, the smaller that window, the better the document matches the query.
Hypothetical: for the query 'grey velvet sofa', a page saying 'grey velvet sofa' has a window of three words. A page with 'grey' at the top and 'sofa' at the bottom has a much wider one.

takeaways.text: A term's BM25 contribution has a saturation point.
k1 calibrates term frequency; 0 makes it binary.
b sets length normalization from none (0) to full (1).
A smaller window of query terms is a better match.

exercise.title: Read your site search settings
steps: Find out which engine runs your site search.
Look up whether it uses BM25 and where k1 and b are set.
Run a generic query and note whether long pages dominate.
Write down one test query set you'd use before changing b.
exercise.prompt_template: My site search runs on [engine] with BM25, k1 = [value] and b = [value]. Long pages [do / don't] dominate generic queries like [query]. Using the textbook's description (k1 calibrates term frequency scaling; b = 1 fully scales by length, b = 0 is none), explain what each change would do and how to test it.

reflection: Do long pages crowd out short answers in your site search?
Where on your pages are the key terms close together?
lessons.whats_next: Next, what this means for writing, and what Google says about keyword stuffing.

lessons.title: Keywords in practice
objectives: Recognise keyword stuffing as Google defines it
Explain why density targets don't help
Apply k1 and b to your own site search

beats.caption: Google: keyword stuffing is filling a web page with keywords or numbers in an attempt to manipulate rankings.
One example: repeating the same words or phrases so often that it sounds unnatural.
Mueller (as reported): the number of times you use a keyword on a page doesn't really matter or make sense.
When you're writing naturally, that usually resolves itself.
On your own site search, k1 calibrates term frequency, and b sets length normalization.

blocks.text: Google's spam policies say keyword stuffing refers to the practice of filling a web page with keywords or numbers in an attempt to manipulate rankings. One listed example is repeating the same words or phrases so often that it sounds unnatural.

blocks.label: Google says
blocks.text: Repetition meant to manipulate rankings is the violation. No saved source gives a safe or ideal keyword density.

Search Engine Journal reported John Mueller saying: 'In general the number of times that you use a keyword on a page, I don't think that really matters or makes sense.' He added that when you're writing naturally, usually that resolves itself automatically. This is a secondary report of a video.

blocks.label: Practitioner judgement
blocks.text: BM25's saturation point is a textbook reason extra repeats add little in that model. It is not evidence of how Google scores.
If you run your own site search with BM25, the two textbook parameters are the dials.

items.text: k1 calibrates term frequency scaling; at 0 the model is binary.

items.lead: Long pages crowding out short ones?
items.text: b controls length: 1 fully scales by length, 0 applies none.

blocks.label: Practitioner judgement
blocks.text: Change one setting at a time and compare results on a fixed set of test queries. The sources don't give recommended values.

takeaways.text: Keyword stuffing is repetition meant to manipulate rankings.
Unnatural repetition is one of Google's examples.
Mueller, as reported, says keyword counts don't really matter.
In your own search, k1 and b are the dials.

exercise.title: De-stuff a page
steps: Pick a page written to a keyword density target.
Highlight every exact repeat of the target phrase.
Rewrite the passages where it sounds unnatural read aloud.
Keep the phrase where a reader would expect it, such as the title.
exercise.prompt_template: Here is my page copy: [copy]. Google's spam policy lists 'repeating the same words or phrases so often that it sounds unnatural' as keyword stuffing. Mark the places where [phrase] sounds unnatural and rewrite them in plain language, keeping the meaning. Don't give me a density target.

reflection: Which of your pages were written to a density target?
Where would a reader expect to see your main phrase?
lessons.whats_next: That's the last lesson. Next, the conclusion pulls the four lessons together.

conclusion.title: Conclusion
conclusion.text: Boolean search only says match or no match, so engines score instead. Bag of words keeps counts and drops order; tf-idf weights a term highest when it's used many times in few documents and lowest when it's in nearly all of them. BM25 caps any one term's contribution at a saturation point, with k1 calibrating term frequency and b setting length normalization. Google's spam policy treats repetition meant to manipulate rankings as keyword stuffing, and no saved source gives a target density. The textbook and review describe methods, not what Google or Bing use.

quiz.title: Course quiz
quiz.intro: You've reached the final quiz for Keyword weighting: tf-idf and BM25. The questions revisit tf-idf, BM25's parameters and keyword stuffing.

multiple_choice_overrides.explanation: Correct: the textbook says b = 1 fully scales the term weight by document length and b = 0 corresponds to no length normalization. Wrong: k1 calibrates term frequency scaling, and tf and idf aren't BM25 tuning parameters.
Correct: the textbook says that in the bag of words model the exact ordering of the terms is ignored but the number of occurrences of each term is material. Order is dropped; counts are kept.

Correct: the textbook says the idf of a rare term is high and the idf of a frequent term is likely to be low. Wrong: tf counts occurrences in one document, and length and b relate to length normalization, not rarity.
